reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: Defined at the molecular level by a single recurrent FGFR3 mutation, the p.Pro250Arg (P250R) substitution, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern
Classically causes uni- or bicoronal synostosis, but the phenotype is highly variable and some carriers are essentially unaffected
Because it is defined by genotype rather than a fixed appearance, molecular testing is essential and clinical overlap with Saethre-Chotzen syndrome is considerable
Sensorineural hearing loss is an important and frequently under-recognised associated feature that should be actively screened for
Macrocephaly, mild developmental or learning difficulties and subtle limb radiographic changes (such as carpal or tarsal fusions) may be present
Females and those with bicoronal involvement tend to be more severely affected than males or those with unilateral synostosis
The recurrent mutation means testing is straightforward and should be offered when coronal synostosis is found without another cause
Craniofacial surgical management follows the pattern and severity of suture fusion, with monitoring for raised intracranial pressure
reference.pathophysiology: Muenke syndrome is caused by a specific gain-of-function change in fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (the P250R substitution) that increases ligand-independent or ligand-enhanced receptor signalling. The heightened FGFR3 activity in the coronal suture drives premature osteogenic differentiation and suture fusion. The same receptor is expressed in the cochlea, which accounts for the associated sensorineural hearing loss, and its wide expression contributes to the marked variability in expression, including non-penetrant carriers.
additionalInvestigations: Targeted molecular testing for the recurrent FGFR3 P250R mutation
Audiological assessment to detect sensorineural hearing loss
Three-dimensional cranial CT to define coronal suture involvement
Developmental and neuropsychological assessment where indicated
Radiographs of the hands and feet to detect carpal or tarsal fusion
MRI of the brain if raised intracranial pressure is suspected
redFlags: Signs of raised intracranial pressure, more likely with bicoronal fusion
Undiagnosed sensorineural hearing loss impairing speech and development
Progressive craniofacial deformity requiring surgical revision
reference.prognosis: Outcome ranges from unaffected carriers to children needing craniofacial surgery; cognition is usually normal or only mildly affected, but unrecognised hearing loss can compromise development, so audiological follow-up is important.
pitfalls: Diagnosing Saethre-Chotzen syndrome clinically without molecular testing, given the overlap
Failing to screen for and treat sensorineural hearing loss
Assuming an affected parent excludes the diagnosis, since expression is highly variable
Neglecting intracranial pressure monitoring in bicoronal cases
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Cranial vault remodelling and suture release by a craniofacial surgical team for coronal synostosis and any raised intracranial pressure
Audiological management of sensorineural hearing loss, including hearing aids and speech and language support
Developmental and educational support with early intervention for learning difficulties
Surveillance for raised intracranial pressure with clinical review, fundoscopy and neuroimaging where indicated
Coordinated multidisciplinary craniofacial follow-up spanning surgery, ENT and audiology, ophthalmology and neurodevelopment
Genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant FGFR3 P250R condition, with testing of at-risk relatives given its variable penetrance
Regular audiological screening, because unrecognised hearing loss can impair development
